newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Coffee, copper trounce market with new highs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Coffee, copper trounce market with new highs.

text.p: The price of coffee futures traded in New York trounced expectations to steam ahead to new contract highs on Thursday as a good technical picture reignited speculative buying.
Elsewhere on the world's commodity markets, London Metal Exchange copper futures hit a fresh one-year high and the price of zinc went to its highest since 1992.
Speculators on the New York market followed through Wednesday's upturn in the price of high quality arabica beans and chalked up new highs shortly after the open.
Many traders had been expecting the market to enter a more stable consolidatory phase.

The benchmark July contract jumped to a new life-of-contract high of 264.00 cents per pound from the previous close of 253.10 cents. It later eased as profit-takers blew the froth of the latest rally.

In London, the price of robusta types for future delivery were more restrained than their American cousins. The July contract rose $55 to hit the day's high of $2,145 a tonne in early trade but ended $5-$10 down.
On Wednesday, the market resumed its blistering rally on news that producer countries had agreed to extend cartel-style export quotas for a year.

The Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) agreed to cap exports for 12 months from July 1 at 52.75 million bags to try to lock in gains from a rally that have taken arabica futures to 20-year highs.
"It's off and running again," said one New York trader. "Specs (speculators) and locals just seem to want to push it higher."

Arabicas were seen to be technically strong after holding above the 239 cents a pound for two days. Support also came from reports of cold weather heading to Brazil, the biggest producer, despite no sign of damaging frosts.
The latest rally prompted the French coffee industry chairman to echo wider worries and announce that coffee consumption would suffer as roasters passed on the higher future prices to the consumer.

Many roasters in Europe and the United States have already raised their retail prices as short South American supply and low stockpiles in consumer countries have boosted futures' by 80-100 percent sine January.

On the London Metal Exchange the price of three-month delivery copper jumped to a fresh one-year high of $2,530 a tonne compared to the previous close of $2,506, denying the market of an expected correction.
Shortages of the red metal, especially in Britain where LME warehouses have stood empty since March 24, have boosted prices.
Zinc also scored fresh gains as trade buying pushed it to a peak of $1,364 a tonne, compared to the previous close of $1,360, its highest level since September 1992.
An LME stocks decline of 3,800 tonnes was supportive.
Both metals eased off later in the day to close a couple of dollars off the peaks.
The price of gold closed some 10 cents firmer at $342.75 an ounce as other precious metals closed slightly weaker.
Benchmark IPE North Sea Brent crude hovered 20-30 cents above the $20 a barrel mark on the strength of gasoline trading in New York.
Wheat futures on the Chicago Board of Trade were a few cents lower on good outlook for crop production this year due to favourable weather.
